note.title: Sub-50 10k by March
paras: Last year I ran the city 10k in 56:40. I went out too fast and walked twice after the 7 km mark. This year I want to finish under 50 minutes.
The plan is to run four days a week and hold 5:30 per km on every run, so my legs learn race pace. If I hold 5:30 for the whole race, I’ll come in just under 50.
Sunday is the long run. I’ll add a kilometre every week until I reach 16.
Strength work twice a week, mostly calves and hips, because that’s where it fell apart last year.
note.brief: I want a strong last 3 km this time, not just a fast first 7.

input.message: What’s the weakest part of this plan now?

output.text:
The two days at 4:55 per km. Last year's 56:40 works out to about 5:40 per km, so "my legs learn race pace" means running 45 seconds per km faster than you've ever held for 10 km, twice a week, from the start. The note doesn't say how long those runs are or whether you can hold 4:55 for any distance yet. Threads 3 to 5 all circle this and none of them got an answer.

It also connects to your goal of a strong last 3 km. Last year fell apart after 7 km because you ran out of endurance at speed, not because the pace was unfamiliar. Two 4:55 days plus a 16 km Sunday leaves one easy day, so you could arrive at the race tired, which is how the last 3 km go wrong.

What does a 4:55 day actually look like in week 1: 3 km straight, 5 × 1 km, or the full 10?

input.target: Skeptic, is going from 56:40 to 49:10 in one season realistic?

output.text: It depends on where you are now, and 56:40 doesn't tell you that. It was a blow-up with two walks, so it measures bad pacing as much as fitness. A 13% drop is big for one season, but some of it may be pacing you already have. Run a hard 5k soon. Under about 23:35 means 49:10 is within reach; around 26 minutes says probably not by March. Also, 4:55 every km leaves you only 50 seconds of slack, so one slow km can cost you the goal.

input.question: Was that my pace or my fitness?

output.text:
Probably both, and they're tangled. Your 56:40 averages 5:40/km. If you went out too fast, the early kilometres were likely well under that, a pace your body couldn't hold, so it gave out around 7 km. That's a pacing error exposing a fitness limit.

Your note leans toward one answer: you put it down to calves and hips, which is a strength explanation. Your splits would settle it. A steady fade from early on points to pace. input.message: What’s the weakest part of this plan now?

output.text:
The weakest part is the one tied to your actual goal. You want a strong last 3 km, but nothing in the plan trains or protects it.

"If I hold 4:55 for the whole race" assumes the pacing problem is solved. Last year's failure was going out too fast, and the plan has no rule for the first 7 km: no target split at 5 km, no cap on early pace. Your 50 seconds of slack is only 5 s/km, so a 4:45 opening is easy to fall into and is the same mistake as last year.

The race-pace days don't say how long they are. Two runs "at 4:55" could be 3 km or 8 km. To be strong at 7–10 km, you need sessions that put 4:55 on tired legs, ending with the hardest part.
